t: ownerless property, whoever takes hold of it acquires it. This chapter and the next deal with the laws of acquiring things that a person made ownerless from his property. The laws of making property ownerless itself were explained in Hilchot Nedarim 2:14-18 (how to make property ownerless and so on).
anything that is ownerless. By itself.

that he not hunt in his fellow's field. When the animal entered there. Although the field's owner does not acquire the animal, nevertheless at the outset it is forbidden for another to hunt there (see Aruch HaShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 273:16). Some explain that the reason is that he has no permission to enter another's field (Maggid Mishneh).

and if he hunted there, he acquired. If he nevertheless hunted an animal that entered another's field, he acquired it (and see below, halachah 4, that there is a case in which the field's owner acquires the animal).
in a vivarium. An enclosure where animals are raised.
a large vivarium, and it requires hunting. That the owner of the vivarium cannot easily catch them there (see Hilchot Yom Tov 2:7).
they belong to the owner of the vivarium. Because they are guarded there.
his trap. A trap for catching animals.
forbidden by rabbinic law. For the sake of peaceful relations (Mishnah, Gittin 5:8; and see also Hilchot Gezelah 6:12).
and if the trap was a vessel. When it has a receptacle, what is caught in it belongs to the owner of the trap by Torah law.
an animal or a bird. That is ownerless.
even though he has no permission to do this, he acquired. As above, halachah 2.

if the field's owner was standing beside his field and said, "My field has acquired it for me," the field's owner acquired. A person's field is considered an unguarded courtyard (where things inside it are not guarded for its owner), and it acquires for a person what is in it when he stands beside it and says, "My field has acquired for me" (see below 4:8-9; Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:8). However, if the field is guarded, the field's owner acquired even if he did not stand beside it and said nothing, for a guarded courtyard acquires for a person even without his knowledge (ibid.).
for this is like a guarded courtyard. For the things in it are guarded for its owner, and therefore it acquires what is inside it (see below 4:9).
and it is not a moving courtyard. A mobile one, and a moving courtyard does not acquire for its owner what is inside it (see Hilchot Mechirah 3:13).

and he fathered no children among Israel after he converted, he has no heirs. For if he had sons born before he converted, they do not inherit him even if they also converted (below 9:7, Hilchot Nachalot 6:10), since after conversion his family lineage is nullified (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:11).
and took possession of his property. Performed an act that demonstrates ownership and acquires the property for him (as detailed below, chapter 2).

and the owner of the adjoining field cannot remove him by paying the price, for this is like a gift. Ordinarily the owner of the adjacent field ("the owner of the border") has priority in buying the field, so if the landowner sells it to someone else, the owner of the border can pay the price and remove the buyer (see Hilchot Shechenim 12:5). However, if a person gives the land as a gift to another, the owner of the border cannot force him to sell him the field (ibid. 13:1), and the same applies to one who takes possession of the field of a convert who died.
and there is a single border between them. A boundary separates the fields.

the one he took possession of he acquired, but the other he did not acquire. Unlike the law of a gift, where if he took possession of one field in order to acquire another with it, he acquired both, since in a gift another person is transferring the fields to him (Maggid Mishneh, and see Hilchot Mechirah 1:19-20).
one inside the other. One inner and one outer.
one who takes possession by a deed etc.. A deed attesting that the land was sold or given as a gift to the convert (Maggid Mishneh).
to plaster it. To cover it.
that is demarcated by its borders. That is defined by boundaries.
in which he hoed one hoeing. He dug a little in it with a hoe or made some other improvement, which in this way acquires the field by the act of possession (see Hilchot Mechirah 1:8, 1:16).

enough for the team to go in the time of plowing and return. The measure of land that a pair of oxen pulling a plow plow in one pass, since it is the way of farmers to plow a field in sections (Maggid Mishneh; and regarding the exact definition of this measure see the various views of the Rishonim on Bava Batra 54b).
and the squill. A plant whose roots go straight down into the ground and do not slant sideways, which people used to plant to mark field boundaries.
that which separates for peah. An area in a field that divides the field into two fields with regard to the obligation to leave peah for the poor (see Hilchot Matnot Aniyim, chapter 3).
and anything that separates Shabbat domains. An area defined by itself with regard to the laws of carrying on Shabbat (see Hilchot Shabbat 14:4).

even if there was between them a domain that divides for divorce documents. An area considered a domain by itself with regard to a woman's acquiring a get, although in the laws of Shabbat it is considered one domain with the area around it (see Hilchot Gerushin 5:9).
a valley. A plain containing several fields.

any place that they presume impure. For example, where the impurity is on a particular side of the valley, and that entire side is presumed an impure place because of the doubt, but on another side of the valley the pure enter without concern. So too regarding a convert's property, one who took possession on one side did not acquire the other side (Or Sameach).
one of the things that divide. Mentioned above, halachot 11-12.

anything called by the name of that convert, he acquires it. He acquires the entire area that was called the field of so-and-so (and above, halachah 10, that he acquires only the plowing measure, speaks of a field not called by the convert's name: Kiryat Melech Rav, Sma, Choshen Mishpat 275:9; and see Maggid Mishneh, Kesef Mishneh, and Even HaEzel, who proposed other answers).
by pulling. The mode of acquisition the Sages instituted for movable property (see Hilchot Mechirah 3:1).

or with money. He can also acquire and transfer with money. For although the Sages instituted that an Israelite has no acquisition in this way, with a gentile there is acquisition (Maggid Mishneh, based on Hilchot Bechorot 4:5).

except by a deed. Together with payment of the money (Hilchot Mechirah 1:17; unlike an Israelite buying land from an Israelite, where a deed alone, or money alone, or taking possession suffices; ibid., halachah 3).
for his mind relies only on the deed. The Israelite fears the gentile will retract, and the Israelite's mind relies only on an acquisition made by writing a deed together with payment.
and he gave the money. But has not yet written a deed.

and before he takes possession of it etc.. But if he already took possession, he acquired it as one who takes possession of ownerless property, and another Israelite cannot acquire it (Maggid Mishneh).
and took possession of it in the way one takes possession of a convert's property. In one of the modes of possession by which one acquires an ownerless field (see below, chapter 2).
and gives the first one the money. For it was by virtue of the first one's money that the gentile left the field and the last Israelite acquired it (Maggid Mishneh).
a law known to the king. A law enacted by the king.
by their word they judge. For the conditions of its application and scope of the king's law, see Hilchot Gezelah 5:11-18.
the property of a convert who has no heirs. Above 1:6.
and a field that a gentile sold to an Israelite and he has not yet taken possession of it. Whose status is that of ownerless property (above 1:14).
in one of the ways of possession we explained in Hilchot Mechirah. 1:8-16.
he acquired. As explained in the previous chapter.
except for eating the fruits. Which is not an acquisition in ownerless property and the like, as explained in the next halachah.

but in ownerless property or a convert's property, even if he ate the fruits of the tree for several years, he did not acquire. In another's property he has no permission to eat its fruits, so eating the fruits is a sign of acquiring the field. Whereas in ownerless property the fruits are permitted to be eaten by anyone, even one who does not acquire the tree or the land, so eating these fruits is not considered an act of acquisition and ownership (Even HaEzel).
as we have explained. Hilchot Mechirah 1:16.

there are many things that if the buyer took possession by them, he has not yet acquired etc.. In ownerless land that has no one to look after it, even minor acts of improving the field demonstrate ownership of the land and acquire it for the one who does them. But in land that has an owner, these acts do not suffice to acquire the land from the owner (Even HaEzel). Some explain that the possession spoken of here with regard to a buyer does not deal with the possession of a buyer at the time of purchase, but with a person who claims he bought the field and relies on having held it for three years, in which case plowing the land is not considered possession of the land (see Hilchot To'en VeNit'an 12:9), whereas with possession by a buyer at the time of purchase, all the acts mentioned in the halachah here are effective for acquisition if done in front of the seller and with his consent (Kesef Mishneh, citing Rabbi Yehoshua HaNagid, a descendant of the Rambam).
palaces. Magnificent palaces and halls.
another plastering... another decorating. For example, there was already plastering or decoration in them and he added to them (some versions read: "one plastering... one decorating").
decorating. Raised figures in plaster.
he acquired. Since he made an improvement and beautification.
one who draws a figure. One who draws something.
one who spreads out coverings. For example, carpets and mats, thereby beautifying the ground (Maggid Mishneh, citing Rabbi Yosef Migash).

one who plows the field in a convert's property acquired. For example, where he plowed a small area, which is considered a sufficient improvement of the land only in ownerless property (but in a sale only plowing the entire field counts as possession, which is what Hilchot Mechirah 1:16 speaks of: Even HaEzel; and in the view of the Kesef Mishneh above, halachah 3, this distinction is unnecessary).
one who splits. Cuts open.
for the work of the tree. For its improvement.
but if his intention is to feed the wood to animals, he did not acquire. Because he did not improve the tree.
from one side. From one direction.
to improve the ground. So that it will be easy to work.
the coarse and the fine. The large and the small.
only the coarse ones. Only the large ones, which are suitable for kindling.
a threshing floor. A place for threshing grain.
one who opens water into the land. He made an opening so that water would enter the field.
to catch fish. That come with the water and remain in the field.
for the first did nothing to the body of the land. This speaks of a case where the first did not dig foundations in the ground (Kesef Mishneh, Maggid Mishneh, and in line with Rabbi Yosef Migash).
for it did not help as a fence. The demarcation of the area made by the very construction of the palaces is not effective as long as it has no doors.
very wide and open through. Open and unfit for use.
one who scatters seed into the furrows. He threw seeds without covering them (Hagahot Maimoniyot and Maggid Mishneh, citing Rashbam).
he did not acquire. For there is no benefit in the upper partition.
the lower partition sank. Sank into the ground.
and thinking they were his. For example, his field was adjacent to the convert's field.
an Israelite's pledge in the convert's possession. That he owed money to the convert and left a vessel with the convert as security for repayment of the debt.

for once the convert died, his lien was nullified. The pledge always belongs to the borrower but is subject to the lender's lien. Therefore, when the lender dies and the debt and the lien are nullified, the pledge is not ownerless but belongs to the borrower.
a convert's pledge in an Israelite's possession. That the convert borrowed money from an Israelite, and the lender took a vessel of the borrower as security for repayment of the debt.
the first one takes from it the amount of his money. The holder of the pledge takes from the pledge the value of the loan.

his courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge. The owner of the courtyard acquires what is in it, and therefore when the convert died, the lender immediately acquired the pledge that was in his courtyard.
as we explained regarding lost property. Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:8.
a convert who died and they plundered etc.. See also Hilchot Nedarim 2:15.
and they plundered. Plundered, took possession.
slaves. Canaanite slaves.
adults acquired themselves as free persons. For they have understanding, and when the convert died they left his ownership and acquired themselves from the ownerless state.
minor slaves are like animals. They have no understanding, and therefore they have no power of acquisition to acquire themselves as free persons.
and we have already explained. Hilchot Mechirah 2:1-4.
who has a son. Who was born to him after he converted and who is his heir.

or whose wife is pregnant. For although one who grants to an unborn child does not effect acquisition (Hilchot Mechirah 22:10), nonetheless an unborn child has a right in an inheritance that comes automatically (Lechem Mishneh).
and with the first, he died etc.. When they took possession of the property upon the first report.
one who takes possession in the second. After it became clear that the first report was correct.

and in the first he did not acquire. Since they initially took possession on the basis of a report, when they heard the report was untrue and returned the property, their possession lapsed (Maggid Mishneh).
in one of the other ways by which movable property is acquired. Detailed in Hilchot Mechirah, chapter 3.
in the way the buyer takes possession. As detailed in Hilchot Mechirah 1:8-16, 2:1-4.
by words. That they agreed between themselves by speech alone.
each of them can still retract. Just as a sale is not acquired by words (ibid. 1:1). However, a person who promises his fellow a small gift and retracts is called untrustworthy (ibid. 7:9).
he gave him the deposit that was deposited with him. The owner of the deposit told the custodian that he is giving him as a gift the deposit that is with him.
as we have explained. Hilchot Mechirah 5:11.

one who says to his fellow, "the maneh that I have in your possession, give it to this one". And the three of them were standing in the same place. For example, Reuven said to Shimon, "Give my money that is with you to Levi."
he acquired. Levi acquired the money, even before it reached him.
whether he gave the maneh to this one for a debt he owed him or gave it to him as a gift. There is no difference whether Reuven's giving to Levi was to repay a debt or as a gift.
whether the maneh was a debt owed to him or a deposit in his hand. There is no difference whether the money had previously been with Shimon as a debt he owed Reuven or as a deposit.
as we have explained. Hilchot Mechirah 6:8.
regarding sale and purchase. See Hilchot Mechirah 1:2, 5:9.
to reveal the matter etc.. To clarify the truth of the matters in case of a dispute between the parties.
to complete the sale. To define it precisely.
as we have explained. Hilchot Mechirah 21:1.
the poorer. The inferior.
such-and-such a portion. For example, half of the field.
for he did not specify the portion. That he did not define its exact location.
anyone who gives a gift on a condition etc.. See also Hilchot Mechirah 11:1.
fruits that he ate. For example, if he received land and ate its fruits.
that the condition be proper. As explained in the next halachah.
we have already explained. Hilchot Ishut 6:1-2, and see Hilchot Mechirah 11:1 (for the details of the laws of conditions see Hilchot Ishut, chapter 2).

a double condition. In which he specifies what will happen if the condition is fulfilled and also what will happen if the condition is not fulfilled (for example, he said, "If you do a certain thing, this object will be yours as a gift, and if you do not do it, you will not receive the object as a gift").

and the "yes" precedes the "no". That he must state the positive part first, what happens if the condition is fulfilled, and afterward state the negative part, what happens if the condition is not fulfilled.
and the condition precedes the act. That he must state the condition before actually giving the gift (see the rulings and opinions).
a condition that can be fulfilled. In practical terms.
the condition is void and it is as if there were no condition. And the recipient acquires the gift immediately.

and anyone who says "on condition that" is like one who says "from now". For example, if he said, "Acquire this gift on condition that you do a certain act," the implication is that if he fulfills the condition, the acquisition takes effect from now (see Hilchot Ishut 6:17-18).

and he need not double the condition. Since it takes effect immediately, the condition does not need reinforcement. Nor does he need to state the condition before the act, but he must stipulate something that can be fulfilled (ibid.).
some of the Geonim ruled like this etc.. See also Hilchot Ishut 6:14.
one who gives a gift on condition that he return it. On the condition that the recipient return it to him.
and eats the fruits. The recipient.
consecrated and returned. That the consecration takes effect, and the ox is also considered returned to its owner.
something fit for him. And since he did not fulfill the condition, because he cannot use consecrated property, the gift and the consecration are void.
it is forbidden for an Israelite to give etc.. This prohibition is derived from the verse "and you shall not show them favor" (Deuteronomy 7:2, Hilchot Avodah Zarah 10:4).
to a resident alien. A gentile who accepted upon himself the seven Noahide commandments, who is permitted to dwell in the Land of Israel (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:7).

as it says, "to the stranger within your gates" etc.. This verse deals with the prohibition against an Israelite eating a carcass, and it says that it is permitted to give it as a gift to a resident alien, but to a foreigner one must sell it and not give it as a gift.
as it says, "a stranger and a resident" etc.. This verse deals with supporting poor Israelites.
to a slave. Canaanite.
acquires the principal. Completely, for what a slave acquires, his master acquires (Hilchot Malveh VeLoveh 2:8).

acquires it for the fruits. That he may benefit from it, but the principal of the gift belongs to the wife, and if the husband dies or divorces her, the wife takes the gift entirely ("nikhsei melog"; see Hilchot Ishut 16:2).
the master acquired and the husband acquired. The condition did not help to remove his right.
in the very principal of the gift, that it be for so-and-so and so-and-so. That he designated it for the use of the wife and the slave.
one who gives all his property to his slave as a gift. He wrote this for him in a deed.
he acquired himself and went out free. Because the slave is included in the property.
he reserved anything at all. He wrote in the deed that he is giving him everything except one item.
for this is not a complete bill of manumission. A slave's manumission document, like a woman's get, must sever the slave from the master completely (see also Hilchot Avadim 7:1).
he acquired nothing. For a slave has no independent acquisition.
and he is silent. When he received it.
protests from the outset. That he said he does not want the gift when it came into his hands.
one who grants to his fellow a gift through another. The giver asked a third person to act as the recipient's agent and acquire for him.
but the recipient etc.. For a similar law regarding sales see Hilchot Mechirah 30:1.
it is doubtful whether this one who was silent had already agreed. One must be uncertain whether his initial silence indicates that he wanted to accept and only afterward retracted.

or this one was silent because nothing had yet reached his hand etc.. And therefore he saw no need or reason to respond, and the fact that he protested in the end proves about the beginning that he did not want to acquire it at all (see also Hilchot Terumot 9:6).
as we have explained. Above, halachah 1.

and if the original owners returned and seized it... it is not taken out of their hands. Like the law of a monetary doubt, where we do not remove from the one in possession, and if the second one took it from the first, he became the one in possession and it is not taken from him (see Hilchot Mechirah 3:10).
he cannot retract. Because Levi acquired it for Shimon.
he can retract until the hundred reaches Shimon's hand. For Shimon acquires the gift only when he actually receives it.
Levi went etc.. In a case where Reuven said, "he goes," in which case Shimon does not acquire until it reaches his hand.
and sought Shimon. Looked for Shimon.

if Shimon died during Reuven's lifetime, he returns to Reuven or his heirs. At the time of Shimon's death Levi's agency was nullified, and he must return the money to Reuven. If Reuven died before receiving the money back, he returns it to Reuven's heirs.

if Reuven died during Shimon's lifetime, he gives the hundred to Shimon or his heirs etc.. At the time of Reuven's death Levi acquires the money for Shimon, because the money is in his hand and there is a commandment upon him to carry out the words of the deceased; therefore in a case where Shimon died before receiving, he gives the money to his heirs (commentators on Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 125:8).

and even though he said the words while healthy. Although the statement of a healthy person does not effect acquisition (unlike the statement of a sick person, called a "shekhiv mera," as below 8:2), nevertheless after his death there is a commandment to carry out his words.
one who acquires a gift for his fellow. He acts as the recipient's agent to acquire for him from the giver.
until the one acquiring is an adult and of sound mind. For only an adult who is not a deaf-mute or mentally incompetent can become an agent (Hilchot Sheluchin VeShutafin 2:2).
even a slave or a maidservant. Canaanite.
since he is not fit for agency ever. A gentile does not become an agent for any matter in the world (ibid. 5:1).
for an Israelite does not become an agent for a gentile. For the law of agency applies only when the principal and the agent are members of the covenant (ibid.).
a minor who is given a pebble and throws it, a nut and takes it. He understands that a stone is worthless and a nut is valuable.
acquires for himself. A minor acquires by Torah law an object given to him as a gift (see Hilchot Lulav 8:10), for when another person transfers it to him he can acquire.
but does not acquire for others. In a matter arising from rabbinic enactment, a minor can acquire for others (Hilchot Eruvin 1:20, Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 5:9).

less than this, neither for himself nor for others. For he has no understanding at all and is like a mentally incompetent person (and if others acquired for him, he acquired, as explained in the next halachah).
but a deaf-mute acquires for himself. A deaf-mute is like a minor: if he is given a gift he acquires for himself, and he does not acquire for others.

as we explained in Hilchot Gezelah. It appears this refers to Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:4, where it is explained that a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor do not acquire lost property for others (and see there, halachah 12, that when one finds lost property they may acquire it for themselves for the sake of peaceful relations; and see further Hilchot Mechirah 29:1 regarding the sale and purchase of a deaf-mute, a mentally incompetent person, and a minor).
one may acquire for a minor even one day old. Although he has no understanding at all and cannot acquire by himself (as above, halachah 7), an adult can acquire from the owner on behalf of the minor.
whether in his presence or not in his presence. Provided that he wants the gift, as explained above, halachah 2.
and a person's courtyard acquires for him without his knowledge etc.. See also Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:8.
in a guarded courtyard. Where the things in it are guarded.
and likewise the four cubits of a person who stands beside them acquire for him. By rabbinic enactment (for the reason for the enactment see Hilchot Gezelah VaAvedah 17:9).

in an alley or at the sides of a public domain or in a courtyard that has no owners. In public places where many people do not stand, so the four cubits can be assigned to one person standing beside them.

and a minor girl, her courtyard acquires for her... but a minor boy does not acquire etc.. The reason for the distinction is that with regard to divorce it is learned from the verse that a get reaching a minor girl's courtyard is considered as reaching her hand, and from this we learn regarding acquiring objects lying there through the acquisition of a courtyard. But for a man, acquisition by a courtyard is learned from the law of acquisition through an agent, and a minor cannot appoint an agent (ibid. halachah 10).

a gift is like a get, in that a person cannot transmit words to an agent etc.. A person can transmit through an agent only a tangible thing. For example, Reuven can give Shimon an object and appoint him an agent to deliver the object as a gift to Levi, but he cannot transmit through an agent the command and instruction to write a get for his wife or a deed of gift for his fellow. Therefore if Reuven asked Shimon to tell Levi to write in Reuven's name a get for Reuven's wife or a deed of gift for his fellow, this has no significance and the document is void (see Hilchot Gerushin 2:5-6).
he said to three. Who are like a court, and nevertheless the words transmitted through them have no acquisitive effect.
to so-and-so and so-and-so. Two witnesses.
like a get. If a person told two people to write a get, they cannot hand over its writing to someone else (ibid.).
the recipient has not acquired it. For the words mean only a promise that he will give it to him.
as we explained. Above 3:1 (that a document must reach his hand), above 5:2 (that he acquires through others).

we are concerned that perhaps he acquired it for him through another. Without the recipient's knowledge (as above 5:2), and therefore the field is presumed to belong to the recipient (for a similar ruling see Hilchot Avadim 6:3).
I wrote. A document by which he transfers the field.
and if it was the recipient's son who said etc.. If the recipient died and his son says this, the matter remains in a state of doubt.
through a third party. In the hand of a third person.
until it becomes known how it was. Perhaps witnesses will come and testify that it was handed over to his father.

and he takes the oath on this, the heset oath. An oath that the Sages instituted for one who denies a claim against him (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 1:3). For example, where the recipient owes money to another person, and does not have enough movable property to repay the debt, and the creditor wishes to collect his debt from this object that is in the recipient's hand, and the recipient claims that it is not his; then he must swear to that (Maggid Mishneh; and see Lechem Mishneh and others who discussed his words; and the Merkevet haMishneh brought further examples of how a heset oath is possible in such a case).
the recipient swears the heset oath and is exempt. He swears against the giver's claim, and need not return the gift to him, since it is in his possession and he has the upper hand.
one who gives a gift, whether healthy or ill. But one who gives instructions because of impending death is judged differently, as below 9:2.
it is nothing. The recipient did not acquire it.

for this one is scheming in order to destroy etc.. For we are concerned that the giver and the recipient are planning that the buyer will pay the giver for the field (since he does not know it was given as a gift), and afterwards the recipient will show the buyer the deed of gift and take the field from him, and the giver and recipient will divide the proceeds between themselves (Yad Ramah, Bava Batra 40b).
one who writes two gifts for one field. Two deeds of gift for the same field.
we have already explained. Hilchot Mechirah 10:3.
that one who submits a moda'a. One who informs the witnesses that the giving of the gift is not of his free will (see ibid. 5:1).
the gift is void even though there is no duress there. Unlike a sale, where a moda'a voids it only if the witnesses know that the seller was indeed under duress.
for in a gift one follows only the giver's intent. For a gift is based on the giver's free and complete will.
one whose circumstances showed that he did not intend to give this gift. It is clear from his actions that he did not really intend to give the gift.
for it is found to be like a moda'a for it. That is, it is similar to a moda'a, which expresses his unwillingness to really give.
and he cried out that he was leaving him empty-handed. That no inheritance would remain for him.
and they hid. They concealed themselves.
and they wrote for him all my property as a gift. In order to calm the son's anger.

and he is like one coerced by his impulse. His impulse tempts him to marry this woman, and so he wrote for her; but he did not resolve in his heart to transfer it to her except until he marries her, after which he would withdraw his gift.
for he revealed his intent in the first gift. That he does not want to give his property to a woman, and does so only because he wants to marry her.
whose date is the same day. The date written in them is identical.
and they are written for one field. In both he transfers the same field.
whoever came first acquired. The one whose document states an earlier hour, the field is his.

whoever they think is inclined to have this field in his hand. That is, they know that the giver's or seller's mind is closer to him, and therefore it is to be assumed that he wants to transfer it to him.

in a document that has no kinyan, but he acquired this field through this document. That is, the transfer of the field was done by the kinyan of a document, by which the recipient acquires the field from the moment the document reaches his hand (above 3:1).

but if each of the documents contained a kinyan. If the transfer of the field was done by kinyan sudar (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there), and the act of kinyan was written in the document as proof that the field was given as a gift, then the recipient acquired the field from the time of the kinyan.
the later one did not cancel the earlier, for it can be said that to add etc.. But if he added nothing, the later one cancels the earlier, as in the next halachah.

that to add a guarantee for him he again wrote it in the form of a sale. A gift is ordinarily given without a guarantee, whereas a sale comes with a guarantee that if the seller's creditor takes the land from the buyer, the seller will compensate the buyer (Hilchot Mechirah 19:3).

for a guarantee is a scribal error. A deed of sale carries a guarantee even if it is not explicitly written, since everyone is accustomed to giving a guarantee, and it is to be assumed that the scribe forgot to write it (ibid.).

to strengthen his power because of the law of the neighbor. In a sale, the owner of the adjacent field has a right of first refusal to buy the field (Hilchot Shecheinim 12:5), but in a gift there is no such right, and the recipient takes precedence over everyone.
if he added anything in the second. Something additional that he did not transfer to him in the first document.

the second document cancelled the first. For when the buyer or recipient accepted the second document, he admitted that there was a flaw in the first document, and the transfer takes effect only from the second date (see Bavli Ketubot 44a).

and he has a guarantee only from the second date. For if a creditor of the seller or giver comes and seizes from him from the first date until the second date, he cannot claim against the seller or giver.
a fixed payment to the king each year. Payment of an annual tax.
if the circumstances showed his final intent. If his true intention can be understood from the context of the matters.
and he heard that he had died. The father heard a report that his only son had died.
and he rose and wrote all his property to another. To receive it after his death.
a public, complete gift. For a gift written in secret is not a gift (above 5:1).

he made him only an apotropos. Appointed to oversee all the property. [Note: the vocalization of the word 'apotropos' follows the Greek original. In Maimonides' own handwritten Commentary on the Mishnah the word appears with several vocalizations: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is unvocalized).]

it is a judgment of his intent that he intended only that his brothers should listen to him. We estimate that the father did not intend to give all his property to this son, but wrote so in order to publicize this son's importance so that his brothers would obey him.
to one son among the sons. One son out of all his sons.
to one of the heirs among the other heirs. For example, where he had no children and his brothers inherit him, and he wrote to one of them.
a betrothed woman. One who is betrothed but has not yet entered the chuppah.

if a promissory note was issued against him and all the property went to pay his debt that preceded the gift. That is, the husband borrowed before he gave his property to his wife as a gift; the property is then pledged to the lender, who can collect it even after it was given to the wife as a gift.
and she does not collect with her ketubah that preceded the debt. Even though her ketubah precedes the debt, she cannot take it from the creditor.

she forfeited every right she had in the property other than this gift. She waived her other rights in her husband's property (for these rights are of no account in her eyes after she has received all his property), and so her ketubah is not valid.

since he made her a partner among the sons and she did not protest, she forfeited her ketubah. Since he gave her a share in the property and she did not protest, that is, she did not say that the property is pledged to her ketubah and she must receive her ketubah, it is to be assumed that she waived the pledge of her ketubah on this property in return for the land she received.
he wrote for her, together with them, only movable property. Which is not so important, and it is reasonable that she would not waive because of it.
or he retained for himself any amount of land. For she relies on this land to collect from it.

and it is an enactment of the Geonim etc.. Since the Geonim enacted that the husband's movable property is also pledged for the ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 16:7), there is therefore no difference in halachah here between retaining land and retaining movables, for she relies on movables as well and did not waive the pledge at all.

for she forfeited her right only to seize from them. To take from the sons themselves; but after he died his father acquired his property, and she can collect her ketubah from property that came into her husband's hands afterwards, as above 5:9.

and she was divorced or her husband died, her gift is void. But while they are married the gift is presumed to belong to the recipient, and therefore the husband does not eat the produce (Hilchot Ishut 22:9).
and she wrote all her property only to smuggle it away from her husband so that he not inherit her. For had she wanted to give a complete gift, she would have retained something for herself.
and if she retained anything. If she kept something for herself.
as we explained. Above 3:9.
these shall be given to the sons and daughters etc.. For it is to be assumed that this is what he meant.
and jewelry. Ornaments.
they were fit for both males and females. Articles suitable for both sons and daughters.
the males take them. For he said 'give these to my sons' (Mel'ekhet Mishneh and others), and some explain that it is because the father's mind is closer to the males (Maggid Mishneh).
one who marries off his eldest son to a virgin in a house, he acquired the house. It was their custom to build a house for the firstborn son who marries and to hold the chuppah there.
and the father retained nothing in this house that he designated for him. That he removed all his belongings from there.

and these matters are like a halachah that has no reason. The manner of the transfer is not understandable, and is like a decree (but the reason for this enactment is understood, as explained shortly; see Tosafot Gittin 14a).
that he retained one vessel in the house for himself. That the father kept for himself.
a storehouse. A warehouse.
and an upper room. An upper floor.
an upper room he did not acquire. For it is not the main part of the dwelling.
and a portico. An entrance room in front of the house.
two houses, one inside the other. An outer house and an inner house.
we have already explained. Hilchot Ishut 23:13-14.
that two people who had a matchmaking between them. That they agreed between themselves on the marriage of their children.
and this one stipulated on behalf of his son. He obligated himself for his son.
they acquired by speech. Without an act of kinyan.
for anyone who stipulates intending to marry. The obligation is conditional on the marriage taking place.
as we explained. Hilchot Mechirah 22:1.
therefore they are not like a document until he collects with them. They do not have the validity of a document with which one may collect from mortgaged property.
whether she herself retracted. That she does not want to enter the chuppah but wishes to receive a get from the betrothal.
the betrothal money is never returned. The man does not get back the money he gave.
and if it was a betrothal made in error. And it became clear that the betrothal never took effect at all.
one who sends gifts to his father-in-law's house. Gifts to the bride and her family after the betrothal.
the betrothal feast. A meal in honor of the betrothal.
a few garments. A few clothes for the bride.

for he sent them only as an adornment. So that his daughter-in-law would look beautiful. And since in the end he did not marry her, the gift returns to him. [Note: Maimonides writes and vocalizes the word 'noi' in his Commentary on the Mishnah as 'no'i'.]

she pays their price at the cheap rate etc.. The foods are valued not at their proper price but at the cheap price (less a third of the price, as explained shortly). This is the value of her benefit from the food, for she could have eaten cheaper food (compare Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 3:2).
for he gave her this gift only with the intention that she would not retract. Therefore if she retracts, she pays also for what she ate.
and anyone who causes the loss of his fellow's money pays. See Hilchot Chovel uMazik 7:7.

for this one does not swear and collect. The amount cannot be determined on the basis of an oath that he spent such and such, but only by witnesses (unlike the damaged and the robbed, who take according to their claim by means of an oath; see ibid. 7:17 and Hilchot Gezelah 4:1).
a widespread custom. Common and accepted.
so that he will be strengthened through them. So that he will be assisted by them.
shoshvinut is not a complete gift. Rather, it is like a loan (see below, halachah 13).
or he was in the city and heard the sound of the tablet etc.. Reuven was present in the city and heard the sound of the drum that was beaten to invite everyone to the wedding.
and he has a grievance against him. Reuven may take offense at Shimon (but this offense has no monetary significance).
more than a dinar up to a sela he sent him, he deducts half for him. If Shimon sent more than a dinar and up to four dinars (a 'sela'), Reuven deducts half of the amount and returns half.

we assess the sender's intent and the measure of the shoshvinut etc.. We estimate Shimon's intention from his character and the amount he sent, and on that basis determine whether to deduct half or the amount of what he ate (the reference to halachah 8 in the middle of the sentence is an error that crept into the printed editions).
if he is an important person, he deducts half for him. Because of his importance he gave generously and does not expect to receive back what he gave.
or he married and died during the days of the feast. And it turns out that Reuven did not rejoice with him all the days of the feast.
Reuven need not return anything to Shimon's heirs etc.. For shoshvinut is not like an ordinary debt, but is given to the groom only for the expenses of his wedding (see above, halachah 2).
or with a deduction if he did not inform him or was not with him in the city. As above, halachah 6.

Reuven's heirs are compelled to return with a deduction. Reuven's heirs are obligated to return the shoshvinut, less what Shimon ate at Reuven's, since Reuven did not eat at Shimon's, as above, halachah 6.
and it is repaid only in its time, like the first marriage. At its proper time, when the second one marries in the same manner as the first married, as above, halachot 2-4.

for he did not send it in order to add for him. One who returns ten dinars does not intend to add and give more than he received by way of interest, for he is not obligated to do so, but gives it as a gift out of joy and friendship. Likewise, the first, who sent one dinar, did not send it on condition that the second add to it.

and the Sabbatical year does not release it. If a Sabbatical year passed before the shoshvin married, the debt is not released (unlike other debts, which are released at the end of the Sabbatical year; see Hilchot Shemitah 9:1).
for he cannot press him and claim from him. He cannot urge him to return the shoshvinut. And a debt that cannot be claimed before the time of release is not released (see ibid. 9:5).
when it returns to the heirs. In a case where the heirs receive the shoshvinut, as stated above, halachah 10.
because it is fit. The shoshvinut was fit to be given to the deceased, but in practice it did not reach him, only his heirs.
and the firstborn does not take a double share of what is merely due. The firstborn receives a double portion only in property that was in his father's possession at the time of his death.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Nachalot 3:1.
a gift. A present, such as food.

or he gave him money when his hand faltered. He gave him money when the recipient was collapsing financially; it is a great mitzvah to give a gift, a loan or other help that will prevent his collapse (see Hilchot Matanot Aniyim 10:7).
and this one swears that it is impossible that you not take, and urged him until he took. From this it is to be assumed that he intended a gift and not a loan.
the lame. One who limps.
the one whose hand was cut off. One whose hand was amputated.

and no kinyan is needed. There is no need to perform a kinyan sudar to transfer the gift (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:5 and the commentary there; this refers to where he gave all his property or explicitly said that it is a shekhiv me'ra gift, as explained below, halachot 15-17).
for the words of a shekhiv me'ra are like written and delivered. Like a document that was written and delivered into the recipient's hand.

and this matter is from the words of the Sofrim. The acquisitive force of a shekhiv me'ra's speech is from rabbinic enactment (for by Torah law speech has no acquisitive significance, only action does; see Hilchot Mechirah 1:1).
even though it acquires only by their words, they made it like one of the Torah. Although its force is only rabbinic, the Sages gave it the force of a Torah-law acquisition.
even on Shabbat one may acquire from him. Even though it is forbidden to perform a kinyan on Shabbat (Hilchot Shabbat 23:12).
for this kinyan is not needed. There is no need for it, for a shekhiv me'ra's gift is acquired without kinyan, and therefore it is permitted to acquire from him even on Shabbat.

and a shekhiv me'ra need not say 'you are my witnesses' etc.. A healthy person who admitted before two people that he owes money to another and did not say 'you are my witnesses' may claim that his words were not said seriously but that 'I was joking with you' (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 6:6-7). But a shekhiv me'ra who admitted a debt that he owes need not say so (Bavli Bava Batra 175a, and see below 9:9).
the fetus acquired. Even though a person cannot transfer to one who has not yet come into the world.
as we explained. Hilchot Mechirah 22:10.
if my wife bears a male, he shall take a maneh. If she gives birth in the future to a male, he will receive one hundred dinars.
a tumtum. One whose sexual organs are covered and it is not apparent whether he is male or female.
an androginos. One who has both male and female sexual organs.

takes the lesser of the two. He takes the minimum amount (one hundred dinars), since he is doubtfully male and doubtfully female (see Hilchot Ishut 2:24-25), and money is not taken out of a person's hand on the basis of doubt.
a shekhiv me'ra to whom they said, 'to whom is your property?'. They asked him to whom he wants to give his property.

and he said to them, it seems that he has a son etc.. I thought I had a son, or I thought my wife was pregnant, and now from your question I understand that I have no son, or that my wife is not pregnant, and so I will give my property to so-and-so (Meiri, Bava Batra 147a).
and it became known that he has a son, or that his wife was pregnant. At the time of the gift, as he had originally thought.
his gift is not a gift. Because it was given on a mistaken assumption.

therefore they collect for the woman's ketubah and for the maintenance of the widow and the daughters etc.. A man who marries a woman undertakes that she and her daughters will receive maintenance from his property after his death, and also undertakes that if she dies before him, her sons will inherit her ketubah (Hilchot Ishut 12:2). These obligations are not collected from property that the husband sold or gave as a gift (ibid. 18:13, 19:9). However, in the case of a shekhiv me'ra's gift they are collected from the property he gave, because the gift takes effect only after death (see also ibid. 19:13; as for the wife collecting her ketubah herself, this reasoning is not needed, for she collects even from property that already belongs to a buyer or gift recipient, ibid. 16:10).
in which a kinyan is written. That it was written in the document that they performed a kinyan sudar on the gift.
perhaps he resolved to transfer it only by a document. By means of a document, and not by speech alone as the Sages enacted for a shekhiv me'ra.
and if they performed a kinyan with him in order to strengthen the recipient's power etc.. That the kinyan is not a substitute for a shekhiv me'ra's gift but its purpose is to add force to the gift.
who wrote all his property as a gift, without specification. Without mentioning that it is a shekhiv me'ra's gift.
and did not retain anything. He did not leave himself anything.
if he recovered, he may retract. If he got up from his illness, the gift is void (see below, halachot 25-26).

and even if they performed a kinyan with him to strengthen his power. Even if the shekhiv me'ra performed a kinyan sudar to add force to the transfer and strengthen the recipient's power (see Hilchot Mechirah 5:11-13).
for he did not give all this etc.. For a person does not give all his property while alive.
this is a gift of part. A gift of part of the property, which is judged differently (as he goes on to detail).

and its unspecified form is like the gift of a healthy person, who acquires from the time of writing. A shekhiv me'ra who gave a partial gift without mentioning that it is a shekhiv me'ra's gift, is not judged as a shekhiv me'ra's gift, which the recipient acquires only after death (as above, halachah 8), but as a healthy person's gift, which he acquires at the time the deed of gift is written (provided that immediately after writing he handed the deed to the recipient, for the transfer actually takes effect only on delivery of the deed, as below, halachah 18).
provided that they performed a kinyan with him. That they performed a kinyan sudar on the property he gives as a gift, to acquire it for the recipient.
for a shekhiv me'ra's gift of part requires a kinyan. It does not have the force of an ordinary shekhiv me'ra's gift, which is acquired by speech alone, as above, halachah 2.
whether he recovered or did not recover. Even if the shekhiv me'ra did not recover but died, the recipient did not acquire if no kinyan was performed.
he did not acquire unless he was strengthening his power, as we explained. Above, halachot 10-11.
do not err regarding a shekhiv me'ra etc.. Do not mistakenly think that such a gift is a shekhiv me'ra's gift.
or they performed a kinyan from the giver. That the giver lifted a cloth and thereby transferred the gift to the recipient.
a sign to set his mind at ease etc.. A good sign and a blessing.

that he gave the property, for it is evident that it is all the property he has. He did not say that he is giving all his property but specified the property he is giving, and as is evident to us, this is all his property.
and afterward it will be a gift of everything. We judge the gift as a gift of all his property, so that if he recovered from his illness he may retract.
they see. They examine in what manner he gave his property as a gift.

if like one distributing, his writing etc.. If it appears from his actions that he intended to give all his property and wanted to distribute it among various people, it is as if he gave all his property at once.

and if like one who changed his mind after retaining, and went back and wrote etc.. If it appears from his actions that at first he intended to give only a certain portion to one person, and afterward changed his mind and decided to give a further portion to another person, until in the end he gave all his property, this is like a shekhiv me'ra's gift of part, except for the portion he gave to the last recipient, which is judged as a gift of all his property.
one who writes all his property to his slave. By this the slave acquired the property and himself (above 3:15).

he may retract regarding the property but may not retract regarding the slave, for he has already gone out with the name of a free man. Regarding the property, we estimate that he intended to transfer only after death, as above, halachah 14; but regarding the slave, we estimate that he intended to free him at the time of writing the gift, since at that time he becomes publicly known as a free man (Maggid Mishneh citing Rashba, Gittin 9a; and see also Hilchot Avadim 7:9).

even though they performed a kinyan with him for part, if he recovered he may retract. Although he transferred part of his property as a gift, and ordinarily such a gift is regarded as a healthy person's gift that cannot be retracted (as above, halachah 15), nevertheless if he recovered from his illness he may retract, because it is apparent from his words that he gave because he thought he was going to die.
one who sails at sea. One who sets out on a voyage.
and one who goes out with a caravan. On a long journey.
and one who goes out in chains. Who is being led in shackles to be executed.
each of these four is like one who instructs because of impending death. Because they are in mortal danger.
a shekhiv me'ra who passed from one illness to another. Who was healed of one illness and afterwards fell ill with another illness.
his staff. His walking stick.
his gift is a gift. The gift he gave during his first illness is regarded as a shekhiv me'ra's gift.
and if not, his gift does not stand. Since his gift was made with the intention that he would die of his illness and he got up from it, his giving is void.
a shekhiv me'ra's gift. In which it is written that the giver is ill and lying in his bed.
until he brings proof. The recipient.
only after his death. The death of the shekhiv me'ra.
and it is not a hidden gift. For in an ordinary gift, if one says to the witnesses 'write in secret and give to him,' it is a hidden gift and not a gift (above 5:1).
one who instructs because of impending death. Where it is evident that he gives his property because of death (see above 8:23-24).

even though it is written without specification, we are not concerned that perhaps it is hidden. Unlike an ordinary gift, where if it is written without specification we are concerned that perhaps it is hidden (as above 5:2).
shall take possession. Shall hold, shall acquire by inheritance.
he has acquired. And he will inherit him alone, even though there are other heirs (see below 12:1, Hilchot Nachalot 6:2).
he did not acquire. For it is doubtful whether these expressions carry the meaning of acquisition.
he takes them by virtue of inheritance. For the difference between inheritance and gift see below 12:4.
where this heir was one of his daughters. That he has no sons, and his daughters inherit him.
he made him only an apotropos. For the father's intent was that all the other sons should obey this son.
as we explained. Above 6:2.
a son whose conception was not in holiness. Whose mother conceived while she was a gentile.
since he is not his heir. For after conversion his family lineage is void (Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 14:11).
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Nachalot 6:10.

for the language of inheritance and gift are the same with regard to a single heir. As above, halachah 5; and when a father gives a shekhiv me'ra's gift to his son, it is to be assumed that he intends inheritance, even though he used the language of a gift (Even ha'Ezel).

and if you say he should acquire, it turns out that this is as if he inherited his father. We do not say that the son acquires the property as a gift because the father gave it as inheritance and not as a gift, and this son does not inherit his father (although if he said explicitly that the giving is not by way of inheritance but by way of gift, the son acquired it, Even ha'Ezel). Some explain that the son does not receive it as a gift because of a decree, so that people will not mistakenly think that a convert inherits his father, for to onlookers it would look like inheritance and not a gift (Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 256).
to a convert among other converts. Who is not his son, and the gift is not like an inheritance.
a deposit in my hand for so-and-so. I am keeping it on behalf of so-and-so, and the object belongs to him.
a debt that I have in the hand of so-and-so is not mine, it is so-and-so's. A sum of money that Reuven owes me is not mine but Shimon's.

and even if the convert admitted to his son whose conception was not in holiness... even if a shekhiv me'ra admitted to a gentile etc.. A son whose conception was not in holiness cannot receive a shekhiv me'ra's gift from his convert father, as above, halachah 7, and likewise a gentile cannot receive a shekhiv me'ra's gift, as below, halachah 10; nevertheless, if the shekhiv me'ra admitted that he owes one of them, his admission is valid, because this is not a gift but an admission that the property belonged to him from the outset.
we do not listen to him. For a shekhiv me'ra's gift is a rabbinic enactment, and where there is a prohibition they did not enact it.
for this is like one who commanded to commit a transgression with his property. For it is forbidden for a Jew to give a gift to a gentile (see above 3:11).
and we free him. We write him a bill of manumission.

for the slave has some of the mitzvot. A Canaanite slave is obligated in the mitzvot that a woman is obligated in and is not like a complete gentile, and therefore it is permitted to free him even though it is forbidden to give a gift to a gentile.
we do for her etc.. We give her satisfaction by having her work only at work she wants to do, and we compel the heirs not to make her work at work she does not want (Hilchot Avadim 6:4).
and the other said, I do not want them. Immediately upon hearing of the gift the recipient said he does not want it.
he was silent and afterward cried out. At first he was silent, and after some time he cried out and announced that he does not want the gift (see also above 4:1 regarding a healthy person's gift).
that he wrote to this one. His property as a shekhiv me'ra's gift.
that he may retract. He is permitted to retract.
whether of part. For example, where he explicitly said that it is a shekhiv me'ra's gift (Kesef Mishneh, and see above 8:15-16).
whether for himself or for another. Whether he wants his property back for himself or wants to give it to another person.
and he acquired for the first. Through another person who acquires the gift on behalf of the first recipient.

the other has no kinyan at all etc.. The kinyan makes the gift absolute; since he gave his gift a double reinforcement (acquisition through another and a kinyan sudar by himself), he surely intended that the gift take effect immediately as a healthy person's gift.
and they performed a kinyan with him to strengthen his power. The kinyan was meant to strengthen his power and not to diminish it (see above 8:10-11).

and he went back and gave some of them to another, and they performed a kinyan with him to strengthen his power. For example, where he specified that he is giving as a shekhiv me'ra's gift (see above 8:16-17).
he gave part of his property and they performed a kinyan with him. According to the law of a shekhiv me'ra's gift of part, which requires a kinyan (above 8:15).

and if he recovered, the first acquired, the second did not acquire. If the shekhiv me'ra recovered from his illness, he cannot retract regarding the first, who received part (as stated there), but regarding the second, who received the rest of the property, the gift is void (as stated there, halachah 14, that a shekhiv me'ra who gave all his property and then recovered from his illness, the gift is void).

if he recovered, he may retract entirely. In the Gemara (Bava Batra 148b) they were uncertain whether these cases are judged as a shekhiv me'ra's gift, and because of the doubt, we do not take the property out of the giver's hand.

if the money itself was still intact, if he recovered he may retract. It appears from his actions that he left the money in case he recovered and wanted to retract from the sale, and it turns out that he sold on that condition.
the giver shall swear the heset oath. An oath that the Sages instituted for one who denies a claim against him (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 1:3).
and the land shall remain in the giver's possession. For the land remains presumed to belong to its known owners.
since he could say they are mine. For he could have claimed that they were his from the outset (if there are no witnesses that he received them as a gift).
he swears the heset oath etc.. And the movable property remains in his hands.
and a gift was found tied to his thigh. A deed of a shekhiv me'ra's gift.

even though it is witnessed and they performed a kinyan with him etc.. Even though it is recorded in the document that the witnesses performed a kinyan from the giver (so that there is no concern of a deed that takes effect after death; see above 8:10-11).

for I say he wrote it and changed his mind. It is possible that he wrote the document properly and afterward regretted and retracted, for we know of the gift only from this document, and the recipients must bring proof that he did not regret before his death.

and if he acquired it for one. That before his death he gave it to one of the recipients through another, for example by saying to him 'what is written in this document shall be given to so-and-so,' or by handing him the document and saying 'acquire this document for so-and-so' (Aruch haShulchan, Choshen Mishpat 250:40); in this case he cannot retract (above, halachah 16).
a promissory note on himself in another's name. That he owes money to another.
and he placed the document in the hand of a third party. He deposited the document with another person.
this is nothing. The document's keeper cannot hand it to the creditor named in the document, lest the writer of the document intended to borrow and in the end did not borrow.
a shekhiv me'ra who said, 'give a maneh to so-and-so'. For example, where he said explicitly that he is giving as a shekhiv me'ra's gift (as above 8:15-17).
and we are not concerned that perhaps he refers to a maneh he has buried. We need not worry that he means a particular maneh whose location is unknown to us.
that I have in the hand of so-and-so. That belongs to me and is in Reuven's hand.
give it to so-and-so. To Shimon.

and he does not need the presence of all three. It is not necessary for Reuven and Shimon to be present at the shekhiv me'ra's instruction (unlike a healthy person, whose statement is effective as a transfer only if all three are present; see above 3:3 and Hilchot Mechirah 6:8).
give the document of so-and-so to so-and-so. A promissory note, which a healthy person can transfer to another only by writing and delivery (see Hilchot Mechirah 6:10-11).
the heir. Of the shekhiv me'ra.
and the heir went back and forgave it, it is forgiven. As explained in Hilchot Mechirah 6:12.

for the acquisition of the proof in the document is rabbinic. From the words of the Sages, but by Torah law one cannot transfer something that serves only as proof and has no value of its own (see ibid.).
if he said this by way of admission and there was no concern of scheming. It is evident from his words that he intends to admit to money in his possession that is not his.
they give. Unlike a healthy person, who even if he said it by way of admission can later claim that he said so only so as not to be considered wealthy (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 7:1).
and a chest. A cabinet.
if like one conveying his words to them. If he said this in the manner and style of a person conveying information to his sons.
and if like one scheming. If it appears to them that he wants to scheme so that they will not take the money, and tells them that the money is not his (see also Hilchot Ma'aser Sheni 6:7).
if they were hidden in the house. This is a place from which that person could not take the money.
in the field, his words stand. Since he could have taken the money for himself, we believe him when he says that their father said the money is ma'aser sheni.
one who was distressed over money that his father left him. An orphan who was toiling to find certain money that his father left behind.
and they told him in a dream, 'it is such and such'. They told him its exact sum.

and the Sages said, words of dreams neither raise nor lower. What is said in a dream makes no difference in practice, and one may not rely on a dream to say that the money does not belong to the son. Even though it had correct details, it may be mixed with incorrect details, and they need not be concerned about them (Meiri, Sanhedrin 30a).

and they swear the heset oath on this. They swear the heset oath that their father said so to them, an oath that the Sages instituted for one who denies a claim against him (see Hilchot To'en veNit'an 1:3).

and the orphans said, 'father went back and said to us, I paid him,' they are not believed. Some explain that the orphans said their father told them 'I paid' after he told them 'give,' and they are not believed since after he said 'give' it is to be assumed he would not pay on his own. Others explain that the orphans said their father retracted what he said, 'give,' and said that he had already paid the debt earlier, and in this they are not believed; but if the orphans said that their father told them 'I paid' after saying 'give,' they are believed (see Shakh and Taz on Shulchan Aruch, Choshen Mishpat 255:5).
for he did not say 'give,' and how did they know that they are obligated to give?. Since he did not say to them clearly to give, perhaps he planned to repay the debt himself.
and they swear the heset oath that they gave. If the creditor claims that he did not receive his debt, the orphans swear the heset oath and are exempt.
he went and found that he had died. The agent reached his destination and discovered that the recipient had died.
if he was alive at the time the shekhiv me'ra gave to him. If the recipient was alive at the time when the shekhiv me'ra gave the maneh to the agent.

for the words of a shekhiv me'ra are as if delivered. Therefore the recipient acquired the maneh immediately when it was given to the agent, and when he died his heirs acquired it (unlike a healthy person's gift, which the recipient acquires only when it reaches his hand, and if the recipient died before it reached him the agent must return it to the giver, as above 4:5).

we do not say whoever comes first in the document acquires. The order of the recipients written in the document or stated by the shekhiv me'ra does not give priority to the first to receive first; rather, all the recipients are equal in this regard, because it appears from his words that he intended to give to all of them at once.

they divide what is found according to what he wrote for them. Proportionally, according to their shares, for it is to be assumed that the giver intended a higher percentage for the one with the four hundred (unlike creditors, who divide equally because the property is pledged to them equally; see Hilchot Malveh veLoveh 20:4).
and if a promissory note was issued against him. Against the shekhiv me'ra's property.
whoever came first in the document acquired. They receive in order, so that the one who precedes his fellow acquires his entire share first, even if nothing is left for the one after him.
he has no collection from those before him. If the last one's four hundred do not cover the debt, he collects from the one with the three hundred.

he said nothing, for he did not transfer to them anything of substance. For the words of a shekhiv me'ra are like a kinyan, and one cannot transfer something that has no substance (see Hilchot Mechirah 22:13-14).
for he transferred to them the body for the fruits. He transferred the body of the house or the tree for the purpose of use or enjoyment of its produce (see ibid. 23:1).

a shekhiv me'ra who said, 'this property to my sons,' the daughters are not included. For it is to be assumed that he does not want to change from the Torah law of inheritance (unlike a healthy person who sends a gift, in which daughters are included, as above 6:14; see Nimukei Yosef, Bava Batra 66b).
and if the name Rav Toviyah became established, he does not take them. For we say that he is not the person he meant.
and if the shekhiv me'ra was familiar with him. Accustomed to him.

if one of them was a Torah scholar, he takes precedence. For it is a great mitzvah to benefit a Torah scholar from one's property, and it is to be assumed that a person about to die wanted to fulfill this mitzvah (Rashi and other Rishonim, Ketubot 85b).

if one was a neighbor and one was a relative, the neighbor takes precedence. As it is said, 'a close neighbor is better than a distant brother' (Proverbs 27:10), and it is to be assumed that he meant Toviyah the neighbor (Bavli, ibid.).
and all his sons are half. Since he did not specify them but equated all of them with so-and-so.

the sons of so-and-so take half, and the first two take half. Because he divided his words into a specific statement ('to so-and-so and so-and-so') and a general statement ('the sons of so-and-so'), it is therefore to be assumed that he wants to give half to each group.
he takes one sixteenth. They give him the smallest of the shares that this wording can be interpreted to mean.
and there is one who ruled that he takes a quarter of the property. In their opinion the expression 'give a portion' means a quarter (for the understanding of the two opinions see the next halachah).
give him a portion in it for the barrel. A portion of the wine in the cistern for his barrel.
he has diminished, and he takes an eighth of the wine. The shekhiv me'ra revealed his intent that he meant a smaller portion, and the recipient takes an eighth of the wine in the cistern.
for a tafiach. A small drinking jug.
and we do not conclude etc.. We do not learn from them.
for that is a sixth of all the property. A sixth of his property, since together with him there are six heirs.
for a person cannot transfer something not in his possession. See Hilchot Mechirah 22:5.
but not wheat and barley and the like. Which are not called movables in common speech.
if he said, 'all that is movable'. Anything that can be moved.
he takes even the lower millstone. Although it is not usually moved, it can be moved.
a Torah scroll has a doubt whether it is included in 'property'. Because it is forbidden to sell it except for Torah study or for marriage (see Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:2).
give two hundred zuz to so-and-so my firstborn son, as is fitting for him. As is proper for him.

he takes them and takes his birthright. It is reasonable to interpret the father's words to mean that he intended to give the firstborn two hundred zuz as is fitting for him to receive for his good deeds, in addition to the firstborn's portion (Meiri, Bava Batra 138a).
if he said, 'for his birthright'. If the father said that the giving of the two hundred zuz is in place of the firstborn's portion.
his hand is on top. He can choose the greater sum of the two.

if he said, 'for his debt,' he has only his debt. Even if the debt is less than two hundred zuz he takes the debt alone and does not take more, because it would appear to be interest (but if he did not say 'for his debt,' it is like a gift unrelated to the loan, and he may take two hundred zuz).
it is as if he gave him two gifts, and whichever of them he wishes he may take. The gifts are not dependent on one another; the recipient may take one of them or both as he wishes.

give four hundred zuz to my daughter in her ketubah. That she will bring in to her husband at her marriage, and it is recorded in the ketubah, and in case of divorce or widowhood she receives the sum back.

if it is the custom of the people of the city to inflate the valuation of the dowry and write a maneh's worth as two hundred. There were places where it was the custom to write in the ketubah double the amount that the bride actually brought, to add to her honor, so that people would think she brings a great deal of money to her husband (Hilchot Ishut 23:11).
and the garments became cheaper. Their price went down, and it is possible to buy the number of vessels or garments that he specified for a smaller sum.
the gain goes to the orphans, and they give her at the cheaper rate. They give her the garments or vessels according to their present price, and keep the difference as profit.
give four hundred zuz, the value of the wine, to my daughter. Four hundred zuz as the value of this wine, that they should sell it and give her the money.
the gain goes to the orphans, and they give her only four hundred zuz. For if they sold the wine for a higher sum, they take the excess for themselves.
who was going out in chains. Who was being led in shackles to be executed.
he takes four hundred zuz from the proceeds of that wine. After they sell it.
to strengthen his power. So that they cannot push him off to other property.
and he left two halves of a palm tree. That he had a partnership in two palm trees.
and these are what he called a palm tree. That the two halves together count as one palm tree.
a house that holds a hundred jugs. Into which a hundred jugs can fit.
for anyone who gives, gives with a generous eye. Generously, and therefore we do not say that he intended to give only part of the house.
every Shabbat. Every week.
a sela. Two shekels.
so that they will not profit too much from the expenditure. That they not increase and expand their weekly expenses, but live frugally.
a shekhiv me'ra who instructed and said etc.. See also Hilchot Avel 12:1.
who instructed and said, 'do not eulogize him'. He asked that they not eulogize him.
we do not eulogize him. For the eulogy is an honor to the deceased (ibid.), and he may waive his honor.
we do not listen to him to spare his sons' money and cast himself upon the community. He may not impose the costs of his burial on the community instead of on his heirs.
for it is forbidden to leave him unburied. For burial is a mitzvah from the Torah, and even if he instructed that they not bury him at all, we do not listen to him (ibid.).
a shekhiv me'ra who said etc.. See also Hilchot Nachalot 6:2.

a shekhiv me'ra who said, 'my son so-and-so shall inherit me'. All this applies when he has no firstborn son. But if he has a firstborn son and said that another son who is not the firstborn should inherit him, his words are void, for he may not uproot the firstborn's share (ibid.).
this one inherits him alone. This applies only if he said it orally; but if he wrote so in a document, his intent is to make him an apotropos, and all the sons inherit equally (above 6:2).

or the other heirs. Who are equal to one another in inheritance. But if he changed from the order of inheritance in the Torah and preferred one person over another who precedes him, his words are void (Hilchot Nachalot, ibid.).

but a healthy person's words do not stand. For from the verse 'and it shall be, on the day he causes his sons to inherit' (Deuteronomy 21:16), we learn that a father may decide how to bequeath the inheritance among his sons only close to his death ('on the day he causes to inherit'; see Bavli Bava Batra 130a-131a and Rashbam there). All this is where he spoke in the language of inheritance, but in the language of a gift his words stand (Hilchot Nachalot 6:5).
the second has only what the first left. The first enjoys the property, and after his death the second will acquire it (see below, halachot 7-8).
the second has nothing. And if the first dies, his heirs acquire the property.

and inheritance has no interruption. Inheritance is not like a gift that can be limited in time, because the heir stands in the place of the deceased and replaces him (see Hilchot Eruvin 2:2), and therefore the inheritance belongs to him absolutely.

whether the first was fit to inherit him. For a healthy person cannot give to whomever he wishes by way of inheritance (as above, halachah 2) but only by way of gift, and even when he gave to his heir it is a gift that can be interrupted.

if he gave the money through a third party or said... they are given only a shekel. Above 11:23 it states that if he said without specification 'give my sons a shekel each Shabbat,' they are given all their needs. Here it is explained that if in addition to this statement he deposited his property with another person (a third party) and it was not in the heirs' hands at the time he died, or he said explicitly that he is not giving to his sons by way of inheritance because he wants so-and-so to receive the property after their death, they are given only a shekel each week (Beit Yosef, Choshen Mishpat 248, Merkevet haMishneh and others).

the property belongs to the first one's heirs. For the second acquires only after the first one's death, and if the second died before the first, he lost his right, and therefore his heirs do not acquire either.
it is forbidden for the first to sell or give their body. It is forbidden for him to sell or give as a gift the body of the property, for the giver wanted the second to acquire it after him.
for the second has neither the body nor the fruits, only what remains. What the first left behind; and when the first sold or gave, he did not leave anything behind.
and even if there were slaves among them and the first freed them. And thereby violated a prohibition (see Hilchot Avadim 9:6).
or vessels, and he made them shrouds for the dead. And thereby forbade them for benefit (see Hilchot Avel 14:21).

he did nothing. Because he deviated from the giver's explicit words; for the giver said to him 'after you to so-and-so' in order to exclude his heirs, that is, that after your death specifically so-and-so receives and not your heirs (but other people who are not his heirs the giver did not explicitly exclude, and therefore after the fact their actions stand; Even ha'Ezel).

and when he dies the second shall acquire. The second has already acquired before the recipients of a shekhiv me'ra's gift. For the recipients acquire by virtue of his death, whereas the second acquires by virtue of the giver's gift, which was given long before but was delayed until the first dies (see Rabbeinu Yonah Migash, Bava Batra 137a).
and they came to court to collect from these properties. The lender or the wife wants to collect from the property that the giver said about, 'after you to so-and-so.'
the court does not have them collect from the body of the property. For it is forbidden for the first to sell or give their body, as above, halachah 8.
rather, from the fruits alone they assess for them. They may benefit from the property toward the debt as long as the first is alive, and after he dies the second takes it.
even if he made them a pledge. He designated them for repayment of the debt.

and she transgressed and married. From this wording it appears that she is forbidden to marry in the first place, and perhaps it means that she is forbidden to marry with the intention of nullifying the second's right to the property, but she may marry innocently (and in some manuscripts and printed editions the reading is: 'and she rose and married').
the husband is a buyer. He is treated like a purchaser, who acquires at the time of marriage the property she brings with her.
she was a married woman... the second takes from the husband's hand. For after her death her husband does not acquire the property; rather, it passes to the second.
on this condition. That after her, so-and-so will acquire it.
for if a husband takes from the hand of a buyer because she sold while she was married. For this is the law for property that a woman brings with her at her marriage (see Hilchot Ishut 22:7).
the second takes from the husband's hand. For the giver intended to transfer to the second and not to the husband, as stated in the preceding paragraph.
and he has only what the first left. The second has only what the first left behind, and when the first sold, he left nothing, as above, halachah 9.

and among the three of them there is none who took out money etc.. Since it would be possible to take the property from the hand of each of the three without end, the Sages ruled that the property remains in the hand of the buyer, since he is the only one who paid for it.
and afterward the old woman died. The giver's mother.

the husband does not inherit that property, because it was due to his wife and the wife acquired it only after she died. The husband acquires only property that was in his wife's possession during her life, and does not acquire property that she was entitled to receive during her life but did not actually receive (see Hilchot Nachalot 1:11).

for 'my heirs' implies even the heirs of his heirs. When he said 'and after her to my heirs,' it is to be assumed that he meant also the heirs of his heirs (but if he said 'and after her to my daughter,' and the daughter died before the mother, the old woman's heirs receive the property, as above, halachah 7; Maggid Mishneh).
and had he said... the husband would inherit it after his wife's death. Because the wife acquired it during her life.
one who writes his property to his son after his death. That the son will acquire it after the father's death.

the body belongs to the son from the time of the document. The body of the property belongs to the son from the date written in the document, even though the father is still alive, for the date in the document proves that he transferred it to him from that time (see below, halachah 15).
and the fruits to the father until he dies. The right of use of the property belongs to the father, for he wrote to his son that he would acquire only after his death.

if the father died and left fruits attached to the ground, they belong to the son etc.. By law the fruits should belong to all the father's heirs, since they grew during the father's lifetime and the father could have picked them; but since the son receives the land and his father's mind was close to him, we assume the father waived his claim to the attached fruits, which are secondary to the land (Meiri, Bava Batra 136a).
or that were ready to be harvested. That they ripened fully and no longer need the ground, so they are considered detached (see Hilchot Mechirah 1:17).
they are appraised for the buyer. Their value is assessed.
when the father dies, the buyer acquires. Even though the son who sold never had the right to use the property.

for the father has only the fruits, and acquiring the fruits is not like acquiring the principal. The right of use that the father had in the property does not mean ownership of the property itself; the property itself belongs to the son already in the father's lifetime, and therefore the son's sale is valid.
he does not acquire it or eat its fruits until after death. He may not use the gift or benefit from it until after the giver's death.
since a date is written in it, and at that time he was alive. The date of writing appears in the deed, and at that time the giver was alive.
the date proves that he transferred it to him during his lifetime. That he transferred the body of the field to him already in the giver's lifetime.
and he acquires only after death. The recipient may use the field and eat its fruits only after the giver's death.
for there is no deed after death. A deed cannot effect acquisition after the giver's death, as above 8:10.
even though the date is in the deed. Even though the date of writing appears in it, which proves that he transferred it from now.
to be on the safe side, they write so. To be extra certain.
this is a complete gift during one's lifetime. The recipient may use it already in the giver's lifetime (and see above 8:19 that for the gift of a person on his deathbed the law is different).
and this is like the embellishments of a deed. Elegant wording so that the deed will be formal and dignified.
